downgraded.text: Burning the vampire's corpse is believed to put a definite end to his evil doings.
downgraded.to_text: The corpse is also burned, and the exhuming, staking and burning together are believed to put a definite end to his evil doings.
downgraded.reason: Machal says 'these acts' (exhuming, staking and burning) together are believed to put an end to the vampire's doings; the draft credited burning alone.

flagged.reason: Ralston prints upuir as 'South-Russian'; the page does not name a people, and reading South-Russian as Ukrainians is the draft's mapping.

flagged.text: Russians / the Ukraine and White-Russia, where Ralston says traditions are most rife within the Russian Empire
flagged.reason: Ralston frames the Ukraine and White-Russia as within the Russian Empire, not as a named people; filing the inhabitants as Russians is a referent choice the page does not fix.
Afanasyev writes 'у нас' and tags the flying belief '(Харьков. губ.)'; the page does not name the people of Kharkov Government, so 'Russians' is an inference from the author's framing.

flagged.text: Karadzic says a vukodlak is a man into whom, according to folk tales, some devilish spirit enters forty days after death and revives him.
flagged.reason: The 1818 OCR reads 'послије сурти 40 дама' (forty days) while the 1852 entry reads '10 дана'; the numeral is OCR-dependent and the two editions disagree.

flagged.text: In the Tambof story, the vampire cannot pass gates on which crosses have been branded, but the gates of a house with no cross open of their own accord.
flagged.reason: Ralston's Tambof story has the stranger say 'Shut tight!' at gates branded with crosses and pass through the uncrossed gates; 'cannot pass' is a fair but interpretive reading of the story.

grade_rationale.text: Ralston's Songs of the Russian People draws on Afanasyev for its vampire material (footnotes to 'Afanasief, P. V. S. iii.' for the Tambof story and the cat-over-corpse belief, and Karadjic's black-colt custom 'quoted by Afanasief'), so Ralston is counted with Afanasyev, not as a further source.
Ralston's Russian Folk-Tales refers its vampire names back to his Songs of the Russian People, p.410, so his two books are one source.
Afanasyev records upyri for the Ukraine and White Russia, with Kharkov Government and Little-Russian beliefs named.
Machal, whose opened pages do not say they draw on Afanasyev or Ralston, describes the vampire and gives Southern Slav beliefs about it.
Karadzic's Serbian dictionary independently records the vukodlak (vampir) for the Serbs: rising from the grave at night, strangling people and drinking their blood.
The 1725 Frombald report independently records a Vampyri case among the villagers of Kisolova.
Ralston names vampire beliefs or names for Russians, Little-Russians, Servians, Bulgarians, Croatians, Slovenes, Kashubes, Poles and Czechs.
With at least four independent authors (Afanasyev, Machal, Karadzic, Frombald) and nine peoples in the verified rows, the entry is widely attested.
